corrections.was: A London lab with no product sells for around $500 million, on the condition that Google create an AI ethics board.
corrections.now: Google buys a London AI lab for a price it did not disclose, reported at $400 million to $650 million, and agrees, The Information reported, to set up an ethics board.
corrections.why: Google confirmed the purchase but declined to give a price, and the papers differed that weekend: Re/code reported $400 million, The Information more than $500 million and the Guardian £400 million, or $650 million. No source calls the ethics board a condition of the sale, which The Information reported Google had agreed to set up, and none says DeepMind had no product: its own site gave its first commercial applications as simulations, e-commerce and games. The plain question on who controls AI repeated the price and the lab with no product.

corrections.was: Citing conflicts with Tesla's own AI work after a failed bid to take control, he walks — and the promised funding largely does not arrive.
corrections.now: OpenAI says Musk will leave its board to avoid a potential future conflict as Tesla turns to AI. It later said he had wanted control of a for-profit OpenAI; by his account, he insisted it stay a nonprofit.
corrections.why: The Tesla reason was OpenAI's, and it named no present conflict: its post of 20 February 2018 said his leaving would eliminate a potential future conflict, and that he would keep donating, which by his complaint he did into 2020. The bid for control is OpenAI's account, given in 2024; Musk's is that others proposed the for-profit and he told them to stay a nonprofit or go it alone. Both now stand, here and on the string from the founding.

corrections.was: The exit forces OpenAI to find capital elsewhere, which forces the structure that everything later breaks on.
corrections.now: Both sides agree a for-profit was under discussion before he left. His exit meant raising the billions without him, through the structure that everything later breaks on.
corrections.why: The exit did not force the structure. By OpenAI's account it and Musk agreed in the summer of 2017 that a for-profit was the next step; by Musk's, Brockman and others suggested one that year. What his leaving settled was that it would be built without him.

source.title: Elon Musk wanted an OpenAI for-profit

corrections.was: With the founding money gone and training costs climbing, a nonprofit could not buy compute.
corrections.now: With most of the pledged billion never paid in, and billions of dollars needed for compute and people in the years ahead, by OpenAI's own estimate, a nonprofit could not raise enough.
corrections.why: The founding money was never there to be gone: by OpenAI's account the nonprofit raised less than $45 million from Musk and more than $90 million from other donors against the billion announced. OpenAI wrote in 2019 that it would need to invest billions of dollars in compute, people and supercomputers.

corrections.now: In March the nonprofit sets up a capped-profit company under its board, its first investors' returns limited to 100 times their money. In July Microsoft invests $1 billion and becomes its exclusive cloud provider.
corrections.why: The cap of 100 times was for the first round of investors; OpenAI expected later rounds to be capped lower. The company was set up on 11 March 2019, four months before the Microsoft investment the card's date marks, and OpenAI's words for Microsoft's part were exclusive cloud provider.

corrections.now: Four years later the board used its control, and was reversed within five days.
corrections.why: The firing card's own sources run from Friday 17 to Tuesday 21 November 2023: the board removed Altman, nearly all the staff signed a letter saying they might resign, and on the fifth day he was back.

corrections.was: When the board finally used its power, the commercial side simply out-voted it with resignation letters.
corrections.now: When the board finally used its power, the staff and the investor reversed it in five days: 738 of some 770 employees signed a letter saying they might resign and join Altman at Microsoft, which had assured them of positions.
corrections.why: There were no resignation letters and no vote. By the Monday 738 of about 770 staff had signed one letter saying they might resign and join the new Microsoft unit, which, they wrote, had assured them of positions, Wired reported; the board took Altman back on the Tuesday.

corrections.why: OpenAI Group is a public benefit corporation, not a conventional one; what became conventional was its stock, OpenAI having said it was moving to a normal capital structure where everyone has stock.

corrections.was: Put a billion dollars into OpenAI in 2019 and about thirteen more after; shipped Sydney; offered Altman a job during the five days.
corrections.now: Put a billion dollars into OpenAI in 2019, and more than thirteen billion in all; shipped Sydney; offered Altman a job during the five days.
corrections.why: The thirteen billion includes the first: CNBC reported at the conversion of 2025 that Microsoft had invested more than $13 billion in OpenAI, backing it from 2019.

corrections.was: It was the structure that fired Altman and could not keep him fired, and it was replaced in 2025 by a public benefit corporation with the nonprofit as shareholder.
corrections.now: It was the structure that fired Altman and could not keep him fired, and in 2025 it gave way to a public benefit corporation whose board the nonprofit appoints and of which it owns 26%.
corrections.why: The nonprofit did not lose control in 2025, as the entry's short line also implied: by OpenAI's account the OpenAI Foundation appoints all of OpenAI Group's directors and holds 26% of its equity. What ended was the cap.

corrections.was: OpenAI withholds its largest model citing misuse risk and starts a still-running argument about openness.
corrections.now: OpenAI holds back the full GPT-2 for fear of misuse, calling it an experiment in responsible disclosure, and releases it in stages over nine months. The argument over openness it sharpened is still running.
corrections.why: The argument did not start here. OpenAI's post quoted its charter of 2018, which had already said safety concerns would reduce its publishing, and pointed to long-running debates over responsible publication in biotechnology and cybersecurity; it called its decision an experiment. The model then went out in four stages, the last on 5 November 2019.

corrections.was: The first time a lab treated its own capability as a hazard in public.
corrections.now: A lab treated its own model as a hazard, in public, and asked the field to take up the arguments over publication that biotechnology and cybersecurity had long had.
corrections.why: No source on the record calls it the first. OpenAI presented the decision as an experiment and set it beside the debates over responsible publication that other disciplines had long had.

corrections.was: Meta tried the gated release OpenAI had pioneered — case-by-case access, research-only licence.
corrections.now: Meta tried the kind of gate OpenAI had kept around the unreleased GPT-2 — case-by-case access, a non-commercial licence for research.
corrections.why: Nothing on the record says OpenAI pioneered gated release. What it did, by its own report, was share the unreleased full model with partner organisations under a non-commercial legal agreement for their research; Meta's LLaMA post describes access case by case under a noncommercial licence focused on research.

corrections.was: GPT-2, GPT-3, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, DeepSeek: all are transformers trained on text to predict what comes next, then adjusted with human feedback to be useful.
corrections.now: GPT-2, GPT-3, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, DeepSeek: all are transformers trained on text to predict what comes next, and the chat models among them are then adjusted with human feedback to be useful.
corrections.why: GPT-2 was trained simply to predict the next word, by its paper, and no human feedback went into it, nor into GPT-3 as first sold; that tuning came to OpenAI's models with InstructGPT in 2022, as the board's own card has it.

corrections.was: A chatbot released to Twitter is taught to post racist content and withdrawn within sixteen hours.
corrections.now: Microsoft's chatbot for young Americans goes live on Twitter and, after what Microsoft called a coordinated attack, tweets racist abuse. It is offline within a day, sixteen hours in by the Guardian's count.
corrections.why: Microsoft's own account, Peter Lee's post of 25 March 2016, puts the tweets down to a coordinated attack that exploited a vulnerability in Tay's first 24 hours, and gives no hour for the shutdown. Sixteen hours is the Guardian's count, from Tay's first tweet to its goodnight; taught was the press's word.

source.title: Learning from Tay’s introduction (Peter Lee)

corrections.was: The first mainstream lesson that deployment context, not model quality, determines behaviour.
corrections.now: What a chatbot says depends on who talks to it. Tay was Microsoft's test of whether a bot like XiaoIce, used by some 40 million people in China, would work as well in America. On Twitter it was turned within a day, and Microsoft called the challenges as much social as technical.
corrections.why: Nothing on the record makes Tay the first such lesson, and Microsoft's post says Tay was not its first chatbot in public: XiaoIce was being used by some 40 million people in China. Nor does Microsoft put the failure outside the system: it writes of a vulnerability and a critical oversight, and of challenges as much social as technical.

source.title: Learning from Tay’s introduction (Peter Lee)

corrections.was: Seven years apart, Microsoft put two chatbots in front of the public and had to rein both in within days.
corrections.now: Seven years apart, Microsoft put two chatbots in front of the public and had to rein both in: Tay within a day, Sydney ten days after launch.
corrections.why: Tay was offline within a day, and Sydney's conversations were capped ten days after launch, as the Sydney card says: not both within days.

corrections.was: A test vehicle strikes Elaine Herzberg in Tempe, Arizona; sensor gaps, disabled braking and inattention compound.
corrections.now: An Uber test car driving itself kills Elaine Herzberg in Tempe, Arizona. It detected her 5.6 seconds out but never classified her as a pedestrian, its emergency braking was off, and its operator was looking at her phone.
corrections.why: The sensors did not miss her. By the NTSB's account Uber's system detected her 5.6 seconds before impact and tracked her to the crash, but never classified her as a pedestrian or predicted her path. The braking was off twice over: the Volvo's own emergency braking was switched off under computer control, and Uber's design left emergency braking to the operator, who was looking at her phone.

source.title: Collision Between Vehicle Controlled by Developmental Automated Driving System and Pedestrian, Tempe, Arizona, March 18, 2018 (Highway Accident Report NTSB/HAR-19/03)

corrections.was: The first death attributed to an autonomous vehicle, and the case that reframed testing on public roads.
corrections.now: Reported at the time as the first pedestrian killed by a self-driving car in the US. Arizona suspended Uber's testing eight days later, and the NTSB called for a federal review before automated test vehicles are allowed on public roads.
corrections.why: It was not the first death in a car driving itself: the Guardian's report of the crash recalls the Tesla driver killed with Autopilot on in 2016. What it reported was the first pedestrian killed. What changed for testing on public roads is now on the card as the record has it: Arizona's suspension and the NTSB's call for a federal review process.

source.title: Self-driving Uber kills Arizona woman in first fatal crash involving pedestrian (Sam Levin and Julia Carrie Wong)

corrections.was: Stanley's team leader went on to found Google's self-driving project, and within a decade the industry Stanley started was testing on public streets.
corrections.now: Stanley's team leader, Sebastian Thrun, went on to found Google's self-driving project, by his own account, and within five years its cars were driving on public streets.
corrections.why: That Thrun founded the project is his own account: his page says he founded Project Chauffeur, later Waymo, and Google's post of October 2010 has its cars already driving from Mountain View to Hollywood Boulevard, five years after Stanley. That the industry was Stanley's to start had no source.

corrections.was: Adversarial training made convincing synthetic faces a weekend project. Three years later the technique was in consumer tools, and the first victims were private individuals.
corrections.now: The network the Reddit user posted in 2017 was not a GAN but an autoencoder: one encoder shared between two faces, a decoder for each. Adversarial training was added afterwards, by tools built on it. The first faces taken were celebrities'; within weeks users were faking people they knew.
corrections.why: The first deepfakes did not use adversarial training. The original network was an encoder–decoder with one encoder and two decoders, by Mirsky and Lee's survey and the faceswap project's account of its original model; adversarial loss was added to it afterwards. Motherboard's first report names celebrities as the first faces used; private individuals followed within weeks. The string's claim and the glossary's entry on GANs now say so.

source.title: The Creation and Detection of Deepfakes: A Survey (Yisroel Mirsky and Wenke Lee)

corrections.was: Named on a subreddit in 2017; a product by 2022; a policy problem the board expects to force provenance rules by 2029.
corrections.now: Named after a Reddit user who posted face-swapped porn in 2017; a free desktop app by January 2018; a policy problem the board expects to force provenance rules by 2029.
corrections.why: Deepfakes were a product within weeks, not by 2022: Motherboard reported FakeApp, an application anyone could use, in January 2018, and Reddit shut the deepfakes subreddit that February. The entry on diffusion models, which tied deepfakes becoming a product to 2022, no longer does.

corrections.now: Google and Timnit Gebru part over a paper

corrections.was: Google demands she withdraw a co-authored paper on the risks of large language models; the AI ethics team implodes in public.
corrections.now: Google tells the co-lead of its ethical AI team to withdraw a paper on the risks of large language models or take its Google authors' names off it. She sets conditions; Google says she resigned, she says she was fired.
corrections.why: Google's demand had an alternative: retract the paper or take the Google employees' names off it, as MIT Technology Review reported and the paper's own acknowledgements confirm. What followed is told two ways, and the card now carries both.

source.title: A leading AI ethics researcher says she’s been fired from Google (Karen Hao)

corrections.was: The industry learns that internal criticism is a career risk. Half the field's safety talent moves to labs of their own.
corrections.now: By Gebru's account, criticism from inside a lab cost her her job; Google says she resigned. Within three months both co-leads of Google's ethical AI team were gone, and a year later Gebru launched DAIR, an institute meant to do the research outside Big Tech's influence.
corrections.why: Nothing on the record says half the field's safety talent left for labs of their own. What is on the record: Google fired the team's other co-lead, Margaret Mitchell, in February 2021, and on 2 December 2021 Gebru launched DAIR, an independent institute. Her reading of her exit is hers, and is now given as hers.

source.title: Press Release: Announcing DAIR

corrections.was: Both events answer the same question — what happens when internal safety criticism collides with product pressure. One ended in a firing; the other in a rival company.
corrections.now: In December 2020 Google and Timnit Gebru parted over a paper on the risks of large language models, and OpenAI announced that Dario Amodei and a handful of colleagues were leaving for a project that would probably focus less on product development and more on research. Neither caused the other: Anthropic was founded by the OpenAI group, and Gebru went on to found DAIR.
corrections.why: Gebru's exit did not scatter anyone into Anthropic, as the string's claim had it: Anthropic was founded by the group from OpenAI, and Gebru went on to found DAIR. That one ended in a firing is Gebru's account, not Google's. The two share a month, not a cause.

source.title: Press Release: Announcing DAIR

corrections.was: Copilot suggested the next line; four years later coding agents ran the terminal, made whole changes and fixed their own failing tests.
corrections.now: Copilot suggested whole lines or entire functions; four years later coding agents ran commands in the terminal, made whole changes and ran the tests until they passed.
corrections.why: GitHub's launch post says Copilot suggested whole lines or entire functions, not only the next line.

corrections.was: In 2025 a federal judge drew a line for books: training Claude on them was fair use, but downloading them from pirate libraries was not, and that half cost Anthropic $1.5 billion.
corrections.now: In 2025 a federal judge drew a line for books: training Claude on them was fair use, but downloading millions from pirate libraries and keeping them was not, and settling that half cost Anthropic $1.5 billion.
corrections.why: The $1.5 billion was a settlement, reached before the trial the judge had set on the pirated copies, not damages awarded; and what he held unjustified was downloading the books from pirate libraries and keeping them in a central library, as the books card says.

corrections.was: Tools that plan, edit and run whole repositories move from novelty to daily use, and software work reorganises around review.
corrections.now: Anthropic, OpenAI and GitHub release agents that edit code across a repository, run its tests and hand the changes back for review. A majority of developers surveyed in mid-2025 did not yet use agents.
corrections.why: Stack Overflow's survey of mid-2025 found AI agents not yet mainstream: a majority of developers did not use them or kept to simpler AI tools. Daily use came later; by its 2026 survey 73% of those using AI coding assistants or agents used them daily. Nothing sourced the work reorganising around review; the makers' own posts show each tool handing its changes back for review. Two plain questions, the primer and two predictions repeated the claim.

source.title: 2025 Developer Survey: AI

corrections.was: The first job where agentic AI became normal infrastructure rather than a demo. Everything else is following this template.
corrections.now: Software is the first work on the board that agents were sold to do rather than shown doing. By 2026 Stack Overflow's survey said AI had become 'less sidekick and more infrastructure' for developers; the board's reading is that other work follows the same course, the task going to the machine and the check staying with a person.
corrections.why: That agentic AI was normal infrastructure in 2025, and that everything else was following the template, had no source. Stack Overflow's survey of 2026 now supplies its own phrase for developers, and the rest is marked as the board's reading.

source.title: 2025 Developer Survey: AI

corrections.was: Software was the first domain with instant verification: code runs or it doesn't. Agents became reliable there first, then generalised into work with slower feedback.
corrections.now: Code can be checked by running it and its tests, and GitHub billed its agent as best at low-to-medium complexity tasks in well-tested codebases. On the board's reading agents took hold in software first, then spread to work whose results take longer to check.
corrections.why: Software was not the first domain with instant verification: games, where the board's self-play cards begin, had it long before. Nothing sourced agents becoming reliable there first; GitHub billed its agent as best at low-to-medium complexity tasks in well-tested codebases.

source.title: GitHub Copilot: Meet the new coding agent (Thomas Dohmke)

corrections.was: Text-to-image tools reach the public within months of each other; one of them ships open weights.
corrections.now: Text-to-image tools reach the public within weeks of each other in the summer of 2022, and one of them, Stable Diffusion, publishes its weights for anyone who accepts its licence.
corrections.why: Midjourney opened its beta on 12 July 2022, OpenAI began inviting a million people to DALL·E on 20 July and Stable Diffusion went to the public on 22 August: weeks apart, not months. Its weights were open to anyone who clicked to accept the CreativeML OpenRAIL-M licence on Hugging Face, which bars harmful uses.

corrections.was: Nothing about image generation could be recalled after this.
corrections.now: Once the weights were out, anyone could copy and run them, and nobody could call them back.
corrections.why: That nothing about image generation could be recalled claimed more than the record holds. What could not be recalled was the published weights, which Stability released for anyone to run.

source.title: Stable Diffusion Public Release (Joshua Lopez)

corrections.was: Both the leaked Google memo and Simon Willison called it the "Stable Diffusion moment" for language models: an open base model, then a flood of community fine-tunes, quantisation and local inference within weeks. The difference is that Stability chose to release and Meta did not.
corrections.now: Simon Willison called it the "Stable Diffusion moment" for language models, and the leaked Google memo said many were calling it that: a capable base model loose, then a flood of community fine-tunes, quantisation and local inference within weeks. The difference is that Stability released its weights to anyone who accepted a licence, while Meta gave LLaMA's to approved researchers, and they leaked.
corrections.why: The memo did not use the phrase as its own: it said many were calling it the Stable Diffusion moment, as Simon Willison had in March 2023. And Meta did release LLaMA, to researchers granted access case by case, before the weights leaked.

source.title: Large language models are having their Stable Diffusion moment

corrections.was: Stable Diffusion had shown that shipping weights with no gate builds a community faster than any API. Mistral took the lesson literally: no gate, no form, a torrent.
corrections.now: Stable Diffusion's weights sat behind a one-click licence on Hugging Face that barred harmful uses, and a community built on them. Mistral went further: no form, no restrictions under its Apache 2.0 licence, a torrent.
corrections.why: Stable Diffusion's first public weights were gated: Hugging Face asked users to share their contact details and accept the CreativeML OpenRAIL-M licence before granting access. Nothing on the record compares the community it built with any API's.

corrections.was: ChatGPT's launch triggers an internal emergency at the company that invented the transformer, and the release brakes come off across the industry.
corrections.now: At the company whose researchers published the transformer, ChatGPT's release leads management to declare a code red, The New York Times reports. Sundar Pichai later says he did not issue one.
corrections.why: The code red is The New York Times's report, from a memo and a recording it obtained; Sundar Pichai told its Hard Fork podcast in March 2023 that he had not issued one, though people had probably sent emails saying there was one. Nothing showed the brakes coming off across the industry. The ChatGPT card's file, Google's file, the string from ChatGPT and the blurb of finding 14 said the same, and now say what the record holds.

corrections.was: Competitive pressure, not capability, is what ends the era of cautious staged releases.
corrections.now: Google already had a chatbot to rival ChatGPT, kept to a test app; competition, not capability, changed its pace. By the Times's account Google and Microsoft took greater risks with their ethical guidelines; both said they had limited their first releases.
corrections.why: Staged releases did not end: Google released Bard to trusted testers and then to users in two countries, and Bing's chat opened as a limited preview. What the Times reported in April 2023 was narrower, Google and Microsoft willing to take greater risks with their ethical guidelines, and the companies answered that their first releases were limited.

source.title: An important next step on our AI journey (Sundar Pichai)

corrections.was: The company that published the transformer watched a competitor turn it into a consumer product first.
corrections.now: The company that published the transformer watched a competitor put a chatbot built on it in front of the public first, while its own, LaMDA, sat in a test app.
corrections.why: Google had put the transformer in a consumer product years before: BERT, one of its first transformer models, went into Search, as Pichai's post on Bard recalls. What it had not released widely was a chatbot.

source.title: An important next step on our AI journey (Sundar Pichai)

corrections.was: Shipping fast meant shipping a model whose personality nobody had stress-tested in public.
corrections.now: Microsoft had tested a chatbot codenamed Sydney in India since late 2020, it told The Verge, and rude replies from a Sydney bot reached its support forums in November 2022; it said the new Bing had to be built in the open.
corrections.why: Sydney had been tested in public. Microsoft told The Verge it began testing a chat feature of that name in India in late 2020, and The Verge found rude replies from a Sydney bot posted on Microsoft's forums in November 2022. Nor was it Google's to rush out, as the string's claim had it: Sydney was Microsoft's, and reached the public before Google's Bard.

corrections.was: David Hilbert asks whether all of mathematics can be mechanised — question ten becomes the seed of computability.
corrections.now: David Hilbert sets out twenty-three problems for the new century. The tenth asks for a process that decides, by a finite number of operations, whether an equation has whole-number solutions.
corrections.why: Hilbert's address, in the Bulletin's translation of 1902, asks for no machine: problem ten asks for a process for one kind of equation, and the methods to show none exists came later, Martin Davis writes. The programme for all of mathematics dates from the early 1920s, as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy records, and Hilbert's file now says so.

corrections.was: The dream of a decision procedure is the thing Turing and Gödel later prove impossible, and in failing, invent computing.
corrections.now: The dream of a decision procedure is the thing Gödel and Turing later take apart — Gödel the programme, Turing the procedure — and to take it apart Turing has to define computing.
corrections.why: Gödel's work of 1931 bears on Hilbert's programme. That no decision procedure exists is what Turing showed, in his paper of 1936, which says the Entscheidungsproblem can have no solution; the card had credited Gödel with it too.

corrections.was: Paris, 8 August 1900, at the International Congress of Mathematicians

corrections.why: Hilbert read ten of the problems in Paris, the tenth not among them by Wikipedia's list, and printed all twenty-three afterwards, as the card's own file says. Charlotte Angas Scott, reporting from the congress, called those he mentioned a selection from a much longer list.

corrections.was: The tenth asked for a procedure to decide whether any polynomial equation has whole-number solutions, and the broader programme — put all of mathematics on a finite, checkable footing — was stated most sharply in 1928 as the Entscheidungsproblem: a procedure to decide any mathematical statement.
corrections.now: The tenth asked for a procedure to decide whether a polynomial equation with whole-number coefficients has whole-number solutions, and the broader programme — put all of mathematics on a finite, checkable footing — was joined in 1928 by its sharpest question, the Entscheidungsproblem: a procedure to decide whether any statement of logic is provable.
corrections.why: Problem ten is for equations with whole-number coefficients, in the Bulletin's translation, and the Entscheidungsproblem, as Turing's paper sets it out, asks for a process to decide whether a formula of logic is provable, not any mathematical statement. The string to Turing's card now says so too.

corrections.was: Gödel showed in 1931 that the programme could not be completed; Turing showed in 1936 that no decision procedure exists, and had to define what a procedure is to do it.
corrections.now: Gödel's theorems of 1931 are generally taken to show that the programme could not be completed; Turing showed in 1936 that no decision procedure exists, and had to define what a procedure is to do it.
corrections.why: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, now on the card, gives this as a reading: Gödel's work, it says, is generally taken to show that Hilbert's programme cannot be carried out. The card had said Gödel showed it.

corrections.was: The tenth problem itself was closed in 1970 by Yuri Matiyasevich, the same way: no such procedure.
corrections.now: The tenth problem itself was closed in 1970 the same way — no such procedure — when Yuri Matiyasevich completed a decade of work by Martin Davis, Hilary Putnam and Julia Robinson.
corrections.why: The result was not Matiyasevich's alone. Martin Davis, one of the four, writes that when Matiyasevich announced his solution in January 1970, it had been known for a decade that the problem's unsolvability would follow from one construction, which Matiyasevich found.

corrections.now: Nvidia built it for scientific computing and games; the researchers who trained networks on it in 2009–2012 were the customers nobody planned for, and ten years after AlexNet Nvidia was selling more to datacentres than to gamers.

corrections.was: In 2025 the examples stopped being demonstrations — an e-mail that made an assistant leak what it had read, a document that steered a coding agent, a web page that told a browsing agent what to do next.
corrections.now: In 2025 researchers showed it in shipped products — an e-mail that could make Microsoft 365 Copilot leak what it had read, a GitHub issue that made an agent leak its user's private repositories, a web page that told Perplexity's browsing agent what to do next. Microsoft said nobody was known to have exploited EchoLeak. In December Palo Alto Networks reported a real case: hidden instructions on a page serving a scam advert, meant to get it past an AI reviewer.
corrections.why: Every 2025 example on the card was a researchers' demonstration: Aim Labs disclosed EchoLeak to Microsoft, whose record lists it as not exploited, and the GitHub and Perplexity attacks were Invariant Labs' and Brave's own. corrections.was: Everything called a neural network descends from this two-page abstraction.
corrections.now: Everything called a neural network descends from this abstraction.
corrections.why: The 1943 paper runs to some nineteen pages, 115 to 133 of volume 5 of the Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics, not two.

corrections.was: IBM's Candide learns translation from bilingual corpora instead of hand-written grammar.
corrections.now: IBM's statistical models learn translation from bilingual corpora instead of hand-written grammar.
corrections.why: The name Candide appears nowhere in the cited article, and it is anachronistic for 1988.

source.title: IBM alignment models

corrections.was: LeCun's network learns digits from raw pixels and is deployed on bank cheques.
corrections.now: LeCun's network learns digits from raw pixels and reads handwritten US Postal Service zip codes.
corrections.why: LeCun's 1989 network read handwritten US Postal Service zip codes; reading bank cheques came with the later LeNet-5.

source.title: LeNet

corrections.was: Brute-force search takes the world chess title.
corrections.now: Brute-force search defeats the reigning world chess champion.
corrections.why: The 1997 rematch was not a title match: Kasparov lost it and remained the reigning world champion.

source.title: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov

corrections.was: A résumé screener trained on a decade of hires learns to penalise women and is abandoned.
corrections.now: A résumé screener trained on a decade of applications learns to penalise women and is abandoned.
corrections.why: The screener was trained on résumés submitted to the company, not on the people it hired, and the difference is the cause of the skew.

source.title: Algorithmic bias

corrections.was: Her co-authored paper on the risks of large language models is pulled; the AI ethics team implodes in public.
corrections.now: Google demands she withdraw a co-authored paper on the risks of large language models; the AI ethics team implodes in public.
corrections.why: The paper was not pulled. Google demanded that she withdraw it or take its Google authors' names off it, and it was published.

source.title: Timnit Gebru

corrections.was: Code completion trained on public repositories ships to millions of developers, and the licensing fight begins.
corrections.now: Code completion trained on public repositories ships as a technical preview, and the licensing fight begins.
corrections.why: Copilot shipped in 2021 as a limited technical preview, not to millions of developers.
